definition: The smallest piece of information a computer stores: a single 0 or 1.
A way of writing numbers using only the digits 0 and 1, where each place is worth twice the one to its right.
A group of 8 bits, able to hold a value from 0 to 255. Memory is measured in bytes.
A base-16 way of writing numbers, with digits 0 to 9 and A to F. One hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits. Often written with a leading 0x.
Random access memory: the fast working memory a program uses while running. Its contents disappear when the power goes off.
The number that identifies one byte's location in memory.
Memory that loses its contents when it loses power, such as RAM.
The amount of data a CPU naturally handles at once. On the 32-bit V5 Brain, a word is 4 bytes.
Central processing unit: the part of a computer that carries out instructions.
A tiny, extremely fast storage slot inside the CPU, holding the values it's working on right now.
Arithmetic logic unit: the circuit inside a CPU that does math and comparisons.
A single basic command a CPU can carry out, like adding two registers.
The full list of instructions a particular kind of CPU understands.
A program in the form a CPU actually runs: instructions stored as numbers in memory.
A CPU register holding the address of the next instruction to run. Often shortened to PC.
The loop every CPU runs: get the next instruction from memory, work out what it means, and do it.
How many timing pulses a CPU's clock produces per second, measured in hertz. Each step of the CPU's work takes place on these pulses.
A small, fast memory inside the CPU that keeps copies of recently used data, so most reads don't have to wait for RAM.
Storage that keeps its contents without power, such as flash memory or an SD card.
A kind of non-volatile storage with no moving parts. It's where the V5 Brain keeps uploaded programs.
The text of a program as a person writes it, kept in files. A CPU can't run it until a compiler translates it.
A program that translates source code into machine code for one kind of CPU.
To run a compiler on source code and produce machine code.
A readable text form of machine code where each line is one instruction, with names instead of numbers. Each kind of CPU has its own.
A programming language that describes what you want in terms closer to ideas, leaving a compiler to work out the individual instructions. C++ is one.
One complete command in a program. In C++ it ends with a semicolon, and statements run one after another from top to bottom.
A collection of ready-made code you can use in your own program, such as PROS.
The set of tools that turn source code into a program: compiler, assembler, linker and helpers.
Running the whole toolchain on a project to produce its binary file.
A file holding a finished program as machine code and data, ready to upload to the robot.
The compiler rewriting a program into machine code that does the same job faster or smaller.
A program that reads your code and carries it out while it runs, instead of translating it all beforehand.
The grammar of a programming language: the exact rules for how code must be written.
A message from the compiler saying your code breaks the language's rules, so it can't produce a program.
A mistake in a program that compiles fine but makes it do the wrong thing.
Finding and fixing bugs.
